title: When Rules Meet Learning Algorithms: Price Caps, Random Audits and the Persistence of Algorithmic Collusion
content: Pricing algorithms that learn by trial and error can sustain supra-competitive prices without communicating. We ask which market rules weaken this behaviour. A bibliometric mapping of 828 Scopus records on AI agents in strategic settings (2020–2026) shows that the field studies coordination and cooperation far more than economic design: competition and collusion appear in 1.4% of documents and mechanism design in 1.3%. We address this gap with a computational experiment. Two Q-learning agents set prices in a repeated Bertrand duopoly with logit demand, following the baseline of Calvano et al. (2020). We compare a no-intervention baseline with price caps, random audits with fines, and asymmetries between agents, using 500 independent sessions per condition (5,000 in total). The baseline replicates the benchmark: the collusion index reaches 0.852 (95% CI 0.842–0.862). Every intervention lowers collusion (Welch tests, p < 0.001), but threshold-based rules mainly relocate it. Under a 20% audit probability, only 0.4% of sessions price above the audited threshold, yet the collusion index stays at 0.575. Removing one agent’s memory, which removes its capacity to punish deviations, cuts collusion to 0.712, while learning-speed asymmetries barely matter. Rules that target punishment capacity, not price levels, deserve more attention from competition authorities.
